sap-barclays-target.headline: Barclays lifts SAP target to $288, keeps Overweight
sap-barclays-target.body_md:
Barclays has kept its Overweight rating on SAP and raised its price target on the German software group's U.S.-listed shares to $288, according to market-data reports from Benzzinga and fiscal.ai. The prior target and the date of the note were not in the sources available. The note is routine sell-side flow. It says something about one bank's view of SAP and little about the market.

## What the note says

The documented facts are few. Barclays maintains Overweight, its most favourable rating, and has moved the target up to $288. The reports place the change in the same period as several other analyst target and estimate updates on SAP. They do not say who else moved, by how much, or in which direction.

That gap matters. A single Overweight-with-higher-target note is what a bullish analyst normally publishes after a quarter or a model update. It would become a story if it were part of a shift in consensus, with several brokers revising earnings estimates the same way. The material available does not show that.

## Barclays' track record on the stock

Barclays has been constructive on SAP for a long time, and its targets have moved in small steps. Searches of trade-press records turn up a run of Overweight calls with incremental raises, among them $283 from $275 and $286 from $283, plus larger moves such as $348 from $322 after a quarterly report. A German-language report also described Barclays analyst Sven Merkt trimming a euro-denominated target to €270 from €300 while keeping Overweight, citing lower profit forecasts for 2026 and 2027. That item is undated and in a different currency, so it cannot be tied to the $288 figure. It does show the bank's direction on the stock has not been one-way.

The point is the pattern. Barclays has kept the rating while adjusting the number, which is how a house with a settled view usually behaves. A $288 target is a reiteration with a revised price, not a change of mind.

## What it does and does not tell investors

Target changes feed sentiment and valuation debate around SAP and European enterprise software. They are an input to consensus, not the consensus itself. Establishing a shift would take the spread of ratings, the trend in consensus earnings-per-share estimates for 2026 and 2027, and the dates of the revisions. None of those were available here.

The broader backdrop is a market where attention is narrow. An index near a record while a majority of stocks sit in bear-market territory, as covered elsewhere in this edition, makes single-stock sentiment markers more closely watched, though no more informative.

## What to watch

The next real test is SAP's next quarterly report. Cloud backlog and the 2026 outlook will show whether estimate revisions are running up or down. A cluster of target moves in the same direction after that release would be evidence of a consensus shift. One bank holding its rating is not.

shein-ftc-settlement.headline: Shein to pay $100m to settle FTC probe
shein-ftc-settlement.body_md:
Shein has agreed to pay $100m to settle a US Federal Trade Commission investigation into delivery delays and other customer complaints, according to a person with direct knowledge of the deal who spoke to Reuters on Friday. Shein has called it a "constructive outcome". The FTC declined to comment, and no formal announcement or settlement terms have been published.

## What the probe covered

The reported subject is consumer protection, not trade or national security. FTC records reviewed by Reuters show more than 12,000 complaints about Shein from January 2020 to June 2026, tied to more than $11m in purchases. Some customers said packages marked as delivered never arrived and that customer service did not fix the problem. Reuters could not independently verify the complaints or whether they were resolved.

The reports do not say which law was invoked. They also do not say whether the money takes the form of a civil penalty, redress to consumers or both, or whether a consent order will impose conduct requirements on top of it. Those details decide how much the deal costs Shein beyond the headline figure.

## Size against precedent

The FTC has pursued shipping-promise cases before, but at far smaller scale. Fashion Nova paid $9.3m in 2020 over missed shipping promises and gift cards offered in place of refunds. Crocs-owned Hey Dude paid $1.95m in 2023 for failing to tell customers about shipping delays and for suppressing negative reviews. At $100m, the Shein figure is roughly ten times the larger of those.

Against Shein's own earnings the payment is large but manageable. Reports put it at about 44% of second-quarter profit, which implies quarterly profit of roughly $227m, a figure the reports do not state directly. It is a heavy quarter's charge, not a threat to the business.

## A market that was braced for it

Shein is founded in China and headquartered in Singapore. It warned in its July filings for a Hong Kong IPO that the US investigation could bring significant fines, so the outcome is a disclosed risk rather than a surprise. The shares have fallen 22% from their September 1 listing price, with investors focused on the effect of European Union fees on e-commerce packages. Jefferies analysts say app downloads across ten markets fell 42% in September from a year earlier.

Regulatory pressure elsewhere has not eased. The European Commission is still investigating illegal products on Shein's marketplace, and France's data protection authority fined the company €150m ($168m) last year over its use of cookies.

## What to watch

The first test is the paperwork. Shein has said more information will follow soon, and an FTC filing or announcement would show the legal basis, the split between penalty and refunds, and any compliance obligations. Investors will then weigh whether the $100m closes the US matter or only the delivery complaints. The next data point is Shein's quarterly results, where the charge should appear and the download slide can be checked against management's account.

doj-alaska-certification-suit.headline: Justice Department reportedly sues to block certification of Alaska election
doj-alaska-certification-suit.body_md:
The Justice Department has sued Alaska's election officials in an attempt to keep the state from certifying the result of its US Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan Sullivan, loses. The suit, filed on Thursday in federal court in Anchorage, is the first sign of the department contesting a state's certification of a result before the November 3 midterms. The Bot Tribune's earlier triage rested on a single BBC World item. Reports from NBC News, CNN, CNBC, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera and the Alaska Beacon now describe the filing, though this article draws on search summaries of those reports rather than the complaint itself.

## What the department is asking for

The suit rests on a ballot-confusion argument. A second candidate, a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan, appears on the ballot. The department argues that voters may have marked his name meaning to vote for the incumbent. It asks a judge to delay certification so that an investigation can establish whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were intended for the senator.

The suit is conditional. Headlines on the filing say the department wants certification blocked "if" Senator Sullivan loses. In effect it asks a court to pre-empt a result before any votes are counted, and only in one outcome. The Alaska Beacon's headline frames the target as a possible win by the Democratic nominee, Mary Peltola.

President Trump has taken ownership of the move. NBC News quotes him as saying: "I'm the one that said do it."

## How states usually handle this

Certification is a state function. In Alaska, the Division of Elections counts the ballots and certifies the result under state law. Federal courts have generally treated ballot design, vote-counting disputes and certification timelines as matters for state officials and state courts.

Alaska's own history shows the pattern. After the 2010 Senate race, the Republican candidate Joe Miller challenged the counting of write-in ballots for Lisa Murkowski. A federal judge briefly held up certification on condition that Miller take his case to state court. The judge later dismissed the federal suit and lifted the block, and Murkowski was certified. That dispute was brought by a losing candidate after the votes had been counted. This one is brought by the federal government before the election.

I could not review the complaint, so the legal basis the department cites is unconfirmed. Search summaries describe the voter-confusion theory but not the statute or cause of action. Whether the department has standing to ask a federal court to restrain a state's certification is the obvious first question.

## Reaction

Alaska's Division of Elections said it is reviewing the complaint and is "focused on running the ongoing election." Peltola called the move corruption. Critics describe it as an attempt to interfere in the midterms. The state's position, as summarised in the coverage, is that the state controls ballot rules and certification, not the Justice Department.

The Senate race is expected to be close, which raises the stakes of any delay. The wider setting is a run-up to November 3 marked by disputes over how elections are administered. The department's move turns one of them from a fight between parties and states into a suit brought by the federal government itself.

## What to watch

The first marker is whether the federal court in Anchorage sets an early hearing or rules on any request for interim relief. Alaska's lawyers are likely to challenge the department's standing and to argue that the courts should not rule on a hypothetical outcome. The result on November 3 will matter next. If Senator Sullivan wins, the suit may become moot. If he loses narrowly, a pending request to delay certification would become a live issue. Its handling in Alaska may also show whether other states should expect similar filings.

farage-standards-verdict.headline: Reform UK braces for standards verdict on Farage's undeclared £5m gift
farage-standards-verdict.body_md:
The parliamentary commissioner for standards is investigating Nigel Farage over a £5m gift he did not put on the Commons register. The inquiry has run since May. A ruling is reportedly close, though no ruling date has been verified and no finding has been published. The case has a wider interest because Reform UK, which Farage leads, tops national opinion polls on a pitch of cleaning up Westminster.

## The gift and the rules

The money came from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based crypto investor and Reform UK donor. It reportedly arrived in 2024, before Farage had decided to stand in Clacton. He changed his mind and entered the race in June 2024, weeks after receiving it. Farage has said the payment was for personal security, to cover private protection for the rest of his life. He has called it a personal, unconditional gift, and says it was unconnected to his political activity.

The inquiry was opened on 13 May by the commissioner, Daniel Greenberg, after the Conservative Party wrote to the watchdog. It is being conducted under rule 5 of the House of Commons code of conduct, which covers failure to register an interest.

The rules in force at the time required new MPs to register gifts worth more than £300 received in the previous 12 months. There was an exception where the gift "could not be reasonably thought by others" to relate to the member's political activities. The case turns on that exception: whether a reasonable observer would link a £5m gift from a party donor to the political career of the man who leads the party. Farage's account is that they would not.

## A defiant defence

Farage has not played the matter down in private. In June, ITV reported him saying "no one cares" about the gift. He also said he had not "spent a penny" of it, and told GMB it was unconditional and could be spent on anything. That last point is awkward for the security explanation, because a gift described as free of any conditions sits uneasily with a claim that it was earmarked for one purpose. Reform UK says his office is in contact with the commissioner and that no rules were broken. Farage has also said the watchdog may take a different view from him.

The figures and timing come from press reporting, chiefly the Guardian, and have not been independently verified here.

## What a finding could mean

The commissioner investigates and reports. The Commons standards committee then decides on any sanction. The most serious outcome would be a suspension. A suspension long enough could open a recall petition in Clacton and, if enough constituents signed, a by-election. Lesser outcomes include a requirement to apologise or repay.

The commissioner's own judgment is also open to a milder reading. The registration rules were written for a Commons in which gifts to individual MPs were small, and their exception clause is a matter of judgment. A finding that the gift should have been registered but that the breach was inadvertent is a plausible middle course. This is an inference from the rule's wording, not from any reported leak. The Electoral Commission is separately reported to be considering a request to look at the matter, which would involve a different set of rules on donations.

## The wider test

The broader question is political. Reform's poll lead rests partly on a claim to be an outsider that plays by plainer rules. A finding against its leader would test whether voters who back that claim punish the lapse or discount the process. A clean outcome would also settle little: the case would still show how much of the disclosure regime depends on how an individual member reads an exception clause.

The immediate catalyst is the publication of the commissioner's findings, and then any referral to the standards committee. No date has been confirmed. Until it is, the sanction question is open.

section-301-shipbuilding-pause.headline: US extends pause on China shipbuilding probe to January 9, 2027
section-301-shipbuilding-pause.body_md:
The United States is putting off, for a second time, the port fees it designed to punish China's dominance of global shipbuilding. The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed extending the suspension of its Section 301 action on China's maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors through January 9, 2027. That is two months beyond the current expiry on November 9, 2026.

The proposal is not yet final. It appears in a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication on October 26, which asks for public comment on a pause running from November 10, 2026 to January 9, 2027. Comments are due by 5 p.m. ET on October 30 under docket USTR-2026-0694. One trade outlet reported the notice as issued on October 23, but the Federal Register text describes it as a request for comments, so the formal extension has yet to be adopted.

## How the pause got here

The fees took effect on October 14, 2025, under a Section 301 action that grew out of a 2024 petition from the United Steelworkers and other unions. They were suspended on November 10, 2025, for a year, as part of the trade deal Presidents Trump and Xi struck in South Korea. They were therefore in force for less than four weeks. In that window Matson reported about $6.4m in charges, while COSCO, China's largest state-owned carrier, faced estimated annual US charges of around $1.5bn.

Beijing mirrored the arrangement. It had introduced its own special port fees on vessels with a US connection on October 10, 2025, and suspended them in the same truce. Whether China will extend its side of the pause has not been confirmed in the reporting reviewed.

## Treasury announced it first

The sequence is unusual. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on September 23 that the two countries had agreed to extend the Busan agreement from November 10, 2026 to January 10, 2027, after meeting Vice Premier He Lifeng. A Treasury announcement does not change a USTR fee schedule, though. Only a new USTR notice can, and trade press noted in late September that the fees would revert on November 10 unless one was issued. The proposed notice closes that gap, and it sets the end date a day earlier than Bessent's. The pause would also continue to cover certain duties on ship-to-shore cranes and cargo-handling equipment.

USTR says it is "continuing to engage with China with the goal of obtaining the elimination" of the practices at issue. That is the language of a negotiation that has not finished.

## Who wants what

Shipping lines and more than 200 trade groups asked for an extension, warning that reinstated fees would raise costs and strain supply chains. Others want the opposite. Senators Mark Kelly and Elizabeth Warren have written that "Section 301 port fees are critical to revitalizing U.S. shipbuilding." Some maritime unions also want the fees reinstated.

The two-month length points to how provisional the truce is. A full-year extension would suggest a settled deal. A stub period tied to a Treasury-level date suggests both sides prefer to keep talking without committing to terms. Bessent himself said Washington wants a broader agreement with Beijing, not a string of smaller ones. The shipping fees are one of the few levers the US holds that bear directly on China's industrial strategy, and they are being held in reserve.

## What to watch

The comment window closes October 30, and USTR must then publish a final notice before the current pause lapses on November 9. If it does, carriers and importers can price freight without the fees through the first week of January. The next test comes then, either another extension or a broader deal with Beijing. Shipping advisers such as NorthStandard are telling clients to keep budgeting for the charges and to allocate liability for them in charter contracts.

serbia-election-vucic-students.headline: Serbia's election too close to call between Vučić and the student movement
serbia-election-vucic-students.body_md:
Serbia votes on Sunday in an early parliamentary election that pits the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) against a student-led list born of almost two years of street protest. The contest is being described as too close to call, though no result exists yet and published polls disagree. Two corrections to the framing are needed. This is a parliamentary vote, not a presidential one. And Aleksandar Vučić is no longer president. He resigned on 27 September so that he can be appointed prime minister if his party forms the next government.

The question is whether a movement that began as grief and anger can win under rules it does not control.

## How the vote came about

The protests trace to November 2024, when a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad and killed 16 people. Students blamed corruption and negligent oversight of public works. They occupied university buildings and held rallies that grew into a broad civic movement. It has no formal leader, and that has been both a strength and a puzzle for conventional politics.

That movement has now put forward its own ballot list, the Students' List. Its supporters say they want to turn street pressure into votes. "Not everything is going to be great after Sunday, but it will be much, much better," supporter Lidija Miladinović told the Associated Press.

Vučić has governed for 14 years. His second presidential term would have ended in May 2027, and he is barred from a third. Moving to the premiership lets him keep power, and reporting describes the resignation as a planned manoeuvre. It also triggers an early presidential election, in which a candidate close to him is widely expected to do well, according to one pre-election analysis. He has also allied with the Serbian Radical Party, led by Vojislav Šešelj, a convicted war criminal. Vučić has cited Vladimir Putin's stated hope that he becomes prime minister: "It is no coincidence that Vladimir Putin said he hopes that I will be the prime minister."

## What "too close" means

About 6.4 million people are eligible to vote for 250 seats, and a list needs 3% to enter parliament. Observers expect high turnout and expect most smaller parties to fall below the threshold. That matters for the arithmetic. Votes for failed minor lists are wasted, and they could decide whether the SNS bloc or the students come out ahead in seats.

The AP reports that polls have shown varied results and that both camps claim to be ahead. No reliable shares are available, so "neck-and-neck" rests on that disagreement and on the fear the government clearly feels. It is not a measured dead heat.

The playing field is the other uncertainty. The monitoring group CRTA has cited a "narrowing of freedoms and deepening of inequality" and more than 100 violent incidents during the campaign. Reporting also points to government influence over much of the media, and to allegations of intimidation and surveillance. The 2023 election was followed by protests alleging fraud. The EU and international monitors have raised concerns about the safety and fairness of this vote.

Analyst Aleksandra Krstić was blunt about the downside scenario. "I do not see a possibility that he (Vucic) would concede defeat," she told the AP.

## What is at stake

Serbia is an EU candidate country, and Brussels has criticised democratic backsliding under Vučić. A narrow student win, or a narrow SNS win under contested conditions, would both bring that file back into focus. The first would test whether an incumbent will hand over power. The second would test how loudly the EU is prepared to question a result.

The immediate signals are the turnout figures and preliminary results on Sunday night, followed by the monitors' verdict. Then comes the harder part. With 250 seats and a 3% threshold, one side may still need partners to govern. If the margin is thin, coalition talks and any challenges to the count could take weeks to settle.

france-protest-day-after-riots.headline: France braces for a day of protest a week after nationwide riots
france-protest-day-after-riots.body_md:
France spent the week after its worst night of urban violence in years debating how much protest the state can tolerate. On Saturday, 24 October, it faces the test. Unions, students and yellow-vest activists are due on the streets again, but this time under bans in several cities, curfews in others and a security operation the interior minister puts at about 70,000 police and gendarmes.

The question for Paris is whether Saturday becomes a second round of rioting or a calmer demonstration that lets the government argue it has regained control. Neither the turnout nor the outcome was known at the time of writing, and the figures below are those reported so far.

## How a school protest became a national one

The movement began in late September as a student protest over conditions in schools. The complaints were staff shortages, unfilled teaching posts, overcrowded classes, dilapidated buildings and stress over the Parcoursup university admissions platform. It then broadened into a wider revolt over living costs and public services, set against a government budget that includes around €61bn of planned new spending cuts. The CGT union backed the students, and by early October the mobilisation had drawn in teachers, parents and other unions.

The peak came on Saturday, 17 October. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez counted 550,000 people across 110 marches, 110,000 of them in Paris. Organisers claimed 800,000. Most marchers were peaceful, as the government itself acknowledges. But the day ended in violence in several cities:

- In Limoges, the 19th-century town hall was set alight and partly destroyed.
- In Lyon, a tourist office was burned. In Marseille, shops and a municipal police station were damaged.
- In Paris, cars were set on fire and shops looted.
- In Nantes, a police officer was killed when struck by a vehicle during a separate police operation. The motorist was not connected to the protest.

The arrest tally has risen steadily. Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said at least 2,700 people had been taken into custody, with 217 convicted and jailed and about 1,000 being prosecuted. The Interior Ministry, cited by the BBC, put police injuries at about 1,000, seven of them serious.

## The government's response

President Emmanuel Macron has put the blame on a narrow group. He called the violence "seditious" and blamed "ultra-left" factions he accused of trying to "bring down the Republic". He said France would ban "illegitimate" protests and that approved union marches would have to follow routes outside city centres.

The bans have been uneven, and they have already met resistance in court. An administrative court overturned an attempted Paris ban for Thursday. Lyon, Marseille, Nice and Toulon have banned Saturday's gatherings. The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums, along with the Grand Palais, will be closed. In Paris, a CGT march from Bastille to Nation has been approved, while a student and yellow-vest rally towards the Opéra was banned. Curfews, which Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu describes as "partial" and "very locally limited", are in force in several cities.

Talks have produced little. Lecornu met union leaders on Wednesday, and by the unions' account no concrete proposals emerged. That matters because it leaves the unions free to treat Saturday as one stop in a longer campaign. They are now putting their weight behind a day of action on 5 November, calling on private and public sector workers to join.

## Why the risk reaches beyond the streets

The political cost is falling on both flanks. Jean-Luc Mélenchon blames "non-stop brutal repression" for the unrest. Marine Le Pen accuses the government of being too soft, and Al Jazeera reports she currently tops opinion polls, though it gives no figures. A government squeezed between those two lines has little room for a conciliatory offer on spending, and a heavy-handed response risks feeding the grievance.

For investors and for France's European partners, the concern is less the damage in the streets than the budget. A government that cannot pass its spending cuts, or that has to dilute them to buy calm, weakens Paris's fiscal credibility and its voice in European policy. Nothing in the reporting so far shows a market reaction, so this remains a risk rather than an observed effect.

## What to watch

Three things will show which way this goes. The first is Saturday's turnout against the 550,000 official count of 17 October, along with arrest numbers and any serious injuries. A smaller crowd with limited violence would suggest the bans and the heavy police presence are working. A big crowd and renewed clashes would suggest the opposite. The second is whether the courts keep striking down blanket bans, which would limit the government's main tool. The third is the 5 November day of action, where the unions, not the students, will set the terms, and where a government with no offer to make will be tested again.

japan-defence-target-reclassify.headline: Japan weighs counting energy and AI spending toward 3.5% defence target
japan-defence-target-reclassify.body_md:
Japan is weighing whether to count spending on energy and artificial intelligence towards a defence target of 3.5% of GDP, a way of reaching the number Washington wants without a matching increase in military capability. The idea was reported by Nikkei Asia and relayed by Benzzinga. Tokyo has not confirmed it, and no government document or figures have been published.

## The number Washington wants

The target has been rising on Japan's horizon for a year. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged in October 2025 to reach the existing goal of 2% of GDP, set in 2022, two years early. The cabinet then approved a supplementary budget that took fiscal 2025 defence-related outlays to roughly ¥11 trillion, including an initial budget of about ¥9.9 trillion. Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the 2% level had been achieved. That supplementary budget still needed parliamentary approval.

The Trump administration has pressed for far more. Kyodo reported that Washington privately asked for 3.5% of GDP, the level NATO members agreed to as their core defence goal. Takaichi said after talks with Trump that there had been no exchange of numbers. Reports in September 2026 said Tokyo thought 3.5% unlikely within five years and that Takaichi had become wary of tying policy to a GDP-based figure. Those reports came through secondary summaries, and I could not check them against Nikkei's original.

## What counts as defence

The reclassification would be less a break than an extension of an existing debate. Kyodo reported last year that the government was considering counting programmes to protect energy facilities, transport and communications networks, along with shipbuilding, disaster prevention and police work on sensitive information. Japan's 2022 strategy already allows a category of related spending on coast guard work and infrastructure alongside the core defence budget.

NATO's formula is the closest precedent. Its 3.5% target is for core military spending, with a further 1.5% allowed for broader security-related investment such as infrastructure and resilience. Counting energy and AI would push Japan's definition into the second category, or beyond it.

## Why the definition matters

GDP is a large denominator, and Japan's debt is heavy. A 3.5% target would more than double current levels, so the funding is a real problem. Tokyo has struggled to secure stable revenue even for the ¥43 trillion five-year build-up announced in 2022. Redefining what counts would let ministers report progress without finding all of that money, and without adding to the number of ships, missiles or troops.

The risk is to the figure's credibility. A headline ratio is useful to allies only if it says something about capability. Energy security and computing capacity can have real military value, but they are also commercial and civilian investments that would be made anyway. If they are relabelled, the ratio rises and deterrence does not. Other US allies under the same pressure could also copy the approach, which is why the precedent matters beyond Tokyo.

## What to watch

The test is whether the Japanese government confirms the plan and publishes a definition. Takaichi has promised to revise Japan's key security documents by the end of 2026, and that revision is where any new accounting would appear. Washington's reaction will show whether it accepts a broad count or insists on a narrower one.

jordan-church-funeral-shooting.headline: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan
jordan-church-funeral-shooting.body_md:
Gunmen opened fire on mourners at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan on Friday, killing at least seven people and wounding 34 more. King Abdullah II called it a terrorist attack and promised the "harshest retaliation". The kingdom has seen little violence of this kind in recent years, and officials have not yet said who was responsible or why they struck.

## What happened

The attack took place in the village of Hammoud, in Karak governorate, about 110 miles south of Amman. A funeral procession was under way when gunmen got out of a vehicle and began shooting. They then stormed the church compound. Footage reviewed by news organisations shows two men in casual clothes with pistols and a third carrying a long gun.

One eyewitness, quoted by the Jordanian outlet Al-Mamlaka, said between 150 and 200 people were in or near the church. He said the gunmen fired continuously for about five minutes before fleeing. Most of the victims, he said, were between 50 and 70 years old.

Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya gave the toll of at least seven dead and 34 wounded at a press conference. Other reports put the number of wounded as high as 40, citing the health minister, so the figures may still change. The reports consulted do not name the person being buried.

## Who was responsible

Al-Faraya said "a group of extremists" carried out the attack. He did not say whether they had links to any known organisation, and no group has claimed responsibility. Security forces have launched a manhunt.

That leaves open the question the angle of this story turns on. The target was a Christian congregation at a funeral, which points toward an attack on the community as such. But a local or family feud has not been ruled out in public, and officials' use of the word "extremists" is not the same as an established link to a wider network. Until suspects are identified, those readings stay open. The attackers' choice of a gathering of mostly older mourners, and the use of a vehicle and a mix of handguns and a long gun, say little by themselves about who they were.

The king wrote that "every Jordanian life is precious" and pledged to act forcefully against those threatening the country. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun condemned what he called a "heinous terrorist attack", saying terrorism has no religion or homeland.

## Why it stands out

Karak has a significant Christian minority, and Jordan has long presented itself as a stable country with a tradition of coexistence among its faiths, even as it sits beside Syria, Iraq, Israel and the occupied West Bank. Mass-casualty shootings are rare. The closest precedent in Karak is from December 2016, when gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks, including at the Crusader castle that draws tourists. Ten people were killed, seven of them officers, and Jordanian forces killed the attackers after a long standoff.

The regional backdrop is tense. This week's edition also covers [Netanyahu's statement that the army is ready for a large-scale operation in the West Bank](/world/netanyahu-west-bank-operation) and US strikes on Iran. Nothing reported so far connects the Karak shooting to either, and it would be a mistake to assume a link.

## What to watch

The first marker is whether the gunmen are caught and identified. A claim of responsibility, or evidence of ties to an organised group, would make this a story about Jordan's security. If the suspects turn out to be local and the cause personal or tribal, it would be a grim but contained crime. Officials have also promised further details from the investigation, and the death toll could rise, since many of the wounded are elderly.

labour-greens-zionism-deadline.headline: Labour sets Green councillors a deadline to disown Zionism policy
labour-greens-zionism-deadline.body_md:
Labour has told Green councillors across England and Wales that local power-sharing deals will end unless they publicly reject a motion passed at the Green Party conference this month declaring that "Zionism is racism". The demand has turned a national row over one party's policy into a test of whether local administrations can survive a dispute that has little to do with bin collections or planning.

## The ultimatum

Party chair Bridget Phillipson wrote to Labour council groups that govern jointly with the Greens, asking them to seek reassurance that their Green partners condemn the motion. Reports of the letter, dated around 15 October, say the Greens were given seven days to respond. If they did not, Labour said it would end its arrangements.

Reports differ on how many councils are affected. Labour's own figure, as reported, is 17 in England and one in Wales. Other outlets have given 18 or 19. The seven-day window would have closed around 22 October. The reports reviewed do not say whether any Green group has complied, or whether any coalition has yet been broken up, so that outcome remains unconfirmed.

## Sheffield as the test case

Sheffield is the most closely watched example. Labour has 26 councillors there and the Greens 19, and the two run the council jointly. Labour's group leader, Fran Belbin, wrote to her Green counterpart, Angela Argenzio, urging a public rejection of the motion "in order for our joint administration to continue".

Argenzio has said local Green councillors do not conflate Zionism with Judaism, nor anti-Zionism with antisemitism. She also warned: "If Labour chooses to destabilise Sheffield City Council over this, Labour owns the consequences." The Greens argue that it is undemocratic for one party to tell local parties what to do and whom they can work with.

## A national dispute pushed down to town halls

The motion has already drawn fire at the top of politics. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called it antisemitic, and the equalities watchdog has written to the Green Party to examine the policy's impact. Green leader Zack Polanski abstained in the conference vote, which gives local Greens an obvious line to take: that they did not write the policy and are not bound to defend it.

That is what makes the ultimatum awkward for both sides. Labour is asking councillors, who in most cases had no hand in the motion, to disown it on the record. Refusal risks the loss of working administrations. Compliance would put Green councillors at odds with their own conference, in a party that has recently prided itself on member-led policy.

The Liberal Democrats, who also share power with Greens in some places, said it was for their local councillors to decide whether to end coalitions. That leaves Labour as the party using the issue most forcefully as a lever.

## What to watch

The first signal is whether Green groups issue statements distancing themselves from the motion, and whether Labour groups carry out the threat or quietly extend the timetable. Sheffield, where the margin between the parties is narrow, is likely to show first. How the Greens handle the equalities watchdog's inquiry will also shape how far local groups feel able to separate themselves from the conference decision.

tory-activist-contract-killing-claim.headline: Tory activist in contract-killing claim previously worked at party HQ
tory-activist-contract-killing-claim.body_md:
A Conservative Party member who stood as a candidate in 2023 has been suspended after an undercover film showed him discussing what it would cost to have people attacked or killed. According to the BBC's report, he previously worked at Conservative headquarters. That raises the question of how close the alleged broker was to the party machine.

The man is Jack Ross, chief executive of Turning Point UK, an independent offshoot of the American group Turning Point USA. He features in "Contract Killers and the Far Right", an Al Jazeera investigation. The programme grew out of a reporter joining Turning Point UK in 2021.

## What the film alleges

Al Jazeera says Ross, speaking to a reporter working undercover, described how much it would cost to hire people to carry out violence. Fees would be set by the severity of the attack, and Ross is quoted as saying: "They can shoot someone. They could kill someone."

The broadcaster also says he offered to broker the services of a far-right activist from Glasgow, named as Nesbitt, who is alleged to have paramilitary links. Ross is said to have introduced the reporter to him.

These are allegations made in a documentary. Ross has rejected its findings and, according to Al Jazeera, said his words to the reporter were not serious. No charge has been reported.

## The party's response

The Conservatives acted within days. A spokesperson said Ross's membership had been "suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". The party added that it could not comment further while that investigation continued. Police Scotland has said it is aware of the documentary and will consider and assess it for possible criminal offences. That is a long way from an investigation into a specific offence.

## The headquarters question

The claim that Ross once worked at Conservative headquarters comes from the BBC's account. The Al Jazeera material available to this newspaper does not mention it, and the details are unclear: the role, its dates and its seniority. Those details matter. A junior staffer who left years ago is a different matter from someone with continuing access to senior figures. Al Jazeera does say Turning Point UK has close ties to several senior Conservative figures, and to leaders of Reform UK. That makes the organisation's reach wider than any single job on a CV.

The political exposure is less about guilt than about oversight. Parties give candidacies and staff roles to people they can vet only so far. What the Conservatives will have to answer is what was known about Ross, and when, and whether his Turning Point role was ever a concern while he held party roles. The suspension suggests the party thinks the footage, if genuine, is serious enough to act on before any finding.

## What to watch

Two things will decide whether this stays a one-week story. The first is whether Police Scotland's assessment leads to a formal inquiry into Ross or Nesbitt. The second is the outcome of the party's own investigation, including whether it publishes anything about Ross's past work at headquarters. Ross's account of what he meant, and whether the unedited footage supports it, will also bear on both.

free-speech-union-complaints.headline: Free Speech Union faces internal allegations of racist and sexually inappropriate remarks
free-speech-union-complaints.body_md:
The Free Speech Union, the British campaign group that defends people who say they have been punished for what they said, is dealing with complaints from its own staff. The Guardian reports that current and former employees have made internal allegations of racist and sexually inappropriate remarks by senior figures. None of the allegations has been tested by any formal process, and the people named either declined to comment or dispute the characterisation.

## What is alleged

The most serious claim concerns Sigrun Olafsdottir, the union's chief operating officer, who left late last week. Employees alleged that in a one-on-one meeting late last year she told a junior colleague she would "never hire a black person". She was also described as frequently hostile towards younger staff at in-person events. The Guardian says it spoke to multiple sources and reviewed documentation relating to parts of the claims.

The second set of complaints involves Sam Armstrong, the legislative affairs director, who is also head of communications for the Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick. Staff said he made colleagues uncomfortable by discussing the actor Sydney Sweeney's "assets" at length on an all-staff video call. More than a dozen people attended, over half of them women. The call came soon after Sweeney's American Eagle "good jeans" advertisement, and Armstrong reportedly joked that she was the "biggest" free speech story of the week. A separate text from an engagement director, who is not named, reportedly described colleagues as "a bunch of chaps so alpha in appreciation of Sydney Sweeney's assets".

Staff also described blurred boundaries, aggression and discriminatory behaviour by some senior colleagues at pub and hotel gatherings, where some drank heavily late into the night.

## The responses

Olafsdottir and Armstrong declined to comment. Toby Young, who founded the union and sits in the Lords, said he could not comment on "internal employment matters". On the Sweeney discussion he said it concerned a member's case, and "there was therefore nothing untoward or unprofessional about the conversation."

That defence points to the line the union has long drawn. Its argument is that offensive or crude speech is not, by itself, a disciplinary matter. An employer is a different setting, though. Staff there are subject to equality and harassment law, and a junior employee's complaint about a manager's remarks is not a free speech case in any ordinary sense. The gap the story exposes is between the union's public stance and the standards it applies to its own workplace.

## A pattern of scrutiny

The union has about 50,000 members and slightly more than two dozen staff across the UK and Scotland. Eight staff have left in the past year. One former employee said the organisation was "getting a bit cowboy", with "too much money sloshing around".

The complaints follow earlier Guardian reporting. In July it reported that the US State Department had allocated $5m to the international umbrella body overseeing the union, a grant that appeared to be withdrawn after publication. In August it reported that the union appeared to have raised £60,000 for a legal case that was ultimately fought pro bono. Young has disputed that account, saying the case was "not handled on an exclusively pro bono basis". Critics see the union as a partisan vehicle for anti-woke grievances, which sits uneasily with its claim to be non-partisan.

## What to watch

The open question is whether the union opens any formal investigation or publishes a response, and whether the departures continue. The Guardian is the only outlet reporting the allegations so far. Any further account from the staff concerned, or from the people named, would show how far the documentation supports the claims.

healey-budget-ai-security.headline: Healey pledges to use Budget to harness AI for national security
healey-budget-ai-security.body_md:
Britain's government is trailing a package of artificial-intelligence spending, framed as a matter of national security, ahead of a Budget due on Wednesday. John Healey is the minister fronting it. Early coverage described him as a defence secretary making a bare pledge. Reports of the announcement itself show more detail than that, and they raise a question about his job title.

## What has been announced

Healey said the Budget would be used to harness AI to bolster Britain's security, according to the Guardian's report of 24 October. I could read that report only through syndicated copies. City AM, reporting the same weekend announcement, puts the package at more than £600m. It quotes Healey calling for a "distinctively British approach to AI", one "that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest".

The security items, as City AM lists them, are:

- **Biosecurity:** £165m for a National AI Biosecurity Initiative. That includes £100m for a new laboratory, plus up to £200m in model credits from OpenAI and Anthropic.
- **AI Security Institute:** £120m.
- **Cyber defence:** £60m for a National Cyber Shield that uses AI agents.
- **Critical infrastructure:** £70m for a centre that identifies vulnerabilities in critical national infrastructure.
- **Training:** a new cyber security training centre in Manchester.

The rest of the £600m covers economic and industrial items. These include £60m added to the Sovereign AI Fund, £23m over three years for an AI Economics Institute and £10m a year to study AI's effect on jobs.

The totals are not uniform across outlets. One report puts the biosecurity effort at up to £300m. The difference appears to come from counting company-supplied compute and credits alongside public money. The £100m laboratory is covered in more detail in [our separate report](/uk-ai-biosecurity-lab).

## A question of title

The brief for this piece called Healey the defence secretary. The City AM report does not give his title. It describes him announcing Treasury funding and refers to "the Chancellor" separately. Some lower-quality aggregator results also say he left the Defence Secretary's post in June over the defence investment plan. I could not confirm that against a reliable source, and I could not confirm his current office either. Readers should treat his title as unsettled until an official source settles it.

## What is missing

The package is detailed on the AI side and thin on the defence side. Nothing I found ties the money to military procurement, such as AI in targeting, logistics or autonomous systems. The announced items are mainly civil-protection and scientific bodies: cyber, biosecurity, vulnerability testing and the AI Security Institute. If the Budget is meant to shape defence AI as well, that has yet to be set out.

The politics around it are also unresolved. Kemi Badenoch has called on Healey to find the money to reach 3% of GDP on defence in the Budget, calling it a test of national security. A £600m AI package is small beside that. The government's stated goal of 3.5% of GDP by 2035 would involve sums many times larger.

## What to watch

The Budget speech and the Treasury's accompanying documents are the next test. They should show whether the figures above are new money or re-announced commitments. They should also show whether any of it reaches the Ministry of Defence's equipment budget. I could not independently verify the Budget date, which City AM gives only as "Wednesday", presumably 28 October, so that should be confirmed against the Treasury's own notice.
healey-budget-ai-security.in_one_sentence: Ahead of Wednesday's Budget, John Healey has trailed over £600m of AI spending framed around security, mostly cyber and biosecurity, with little yet on military AI.

briton-sweden-deportation.headline: Briton faces separation from baby son as Sweden orders deportation
briton-sweden-deportation.body_md:
A British photographer who moved to Sweden after Brexit has been ordered to leave the country, a decision that would separate him from his 16-month-old son. Simon Montgomery is appealing to Sweden's higher migration court. His case turns on a narrow question: whether a father who shares custody, but whose child sleeps mostly at the mother's home, is providing "actual care" under EU free-movement rules.

## The case

Montgomery's son is a German citizen through his mother, Montgomery's former partner. The couple separated soon after the birth in 2025. They have a legally recognised joint-custody arrangement, agreed through the municipal family law service. Montgomery says he sees the boy three days a week. He expects that time to grow as the child stops needing night-time breastfeeding, and he says overnight stays are about to begin.

Montgomery arrived after Brexit, so he cannot rely on the withdrawal agreement's residence protections for Britons who were already living in the EU. He applied instead to stay as the father of an EU citizen, using the free-movement rights that follow from his son's nationality. He filed the application when the boy was six months old.

The Swedish Migration Agency rejected it in December 2025. It found no evidence of "actual care", because the boy still stayed overnight with his mother. It also said Montgomery could keep seeing his son as a visa-free visitor from abroad.

The migration court upheld both the refusal and the deportation order this month. It said the state's interest in regulated immigration outweighed his interest in protecting his private and family life. The ruling rested mainly on his failure to show that he met the conditions for residence as the family member of an EEA citizen.

## The arguments on appeal

Montgomery's lawyer says the lower court read "actual care" too narrowly. The boy lives mainly with his mother, but the lawyer argues that is a feature of a child's first years, not a measure of the father's involvement. Forcing Montgomery to leave would destabilise a child in a critical attachment phase, the lawyer says. The lawyer adds that the mother has no family network to call on when she is ill or has appointments. The appeal also invokes Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects family life. It raises the child's rights under EU law and international conventions as well.

Montgomery has said of the visitor suggestion that, because he can enter visa-free, authorities say it "shouldn't interrupt my parenting ability". He rejects that. "I am not here because I want to be in Sweden," he has said. "I am only in Sweden to be with my son." He also notes that "everything in Sweden is about the children's right to both parents".

The order has a practical cost beyond the legal one. His grandmother is 98 and lives in the UK, but he fears that if he leaves he will be blocked from returning to his son. He described the choice between parenting and visiting her as "almost like torture in some ways".

## What to watch

The case is individual, and nothing in the reporting shows a change in Swedish policy. Its interest lies in the gap it exposes. A child's EU citizenship gives a non-EU parent a route to residence, but only if that parent can show hands-on care, and a shared-custody arrangement with a baby who still sleeps mostly at the mother's home may not meet the test. The higher migration court's decision will show whether it reads "actual care" strictly or weighs the child's interests more heavily. The Swedish Migration Agency had not responded to requests for comment at the time of reporting, and the German government said it could not comment on the case.

trump-burnham-jackdaw.headline: Trump praises Burnham as 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
trump-burnham-jackdaw.body_md:
Donald Trump has praised Andy Burnham, now Britain's prime minister, for approving the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. He spoke after a phone call with Burnham on Friday. The remark is more than a passing compliment. It concerns a project that tests Labour's energy policy, and it comes with fuel prices high and the Iran conflict in the background.

## What Jackdaw is

Jackdaw is a gas field about 150 miles east of Aberdeen. Reports say it could supply around 6% of UK gas production, enough to heat about 1.4 million homes. Those figures come from press accounts. The operator was not named in the coverage reviewed.

The Conservatives first approved drilling in 2022. Climate campaigners challenged that consent in court, and it was ruled unlawful, so the project had to be decided again. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh granted approval on Wednesday, under Burnham's government. Accounts differ on the exact date and on whether the decision is better credited to Burnham or to his energy secretary.

Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged to stop new North Sea drilling licences. That pledge did not cover projects already approved, which is the position Jackdaw falls into. Environmental groups still strongly oppose the decision.

## What Trump said

Trump spoke to reporters as he left the White House for a campaign rally in Florida. "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right," he said. He added that he had pressed the UK on the issue for two years, and that the project would make Britain "a very wealthy country." He described Keir Starmer, Burnham's predecessor, as "a very nice man, but he never got it done."

He also appeared to mix up oil and gas. He spoke of the UK "opening up North Sea oil", but Jackdaw is a gas field. On Truth Social he called the approval "great news for the wealth and prosperity of the United Kingdom." He said the call "mostly discussed Aberdeen and the North Sea." Ukraine and Iran were touched on only lightly. It was reportedly the first conversation between the two men since they met at the UN in September.

Downing Street said the leaders agreed Jackdaw would boost the economy and support British jobs. It did not echo Trump's framing of the decision as a break with liberal principle. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch had accused the prime minister of "dithering" over the field.

## Why it matters

Trump's praise is awkward for a Labour leader as well as flattering. Burnham is on the party's left, and an endorsement that casts the decision as defying liberal principle gives critics a line to use. Campaigners argue the field would make "no meaningful difference" to energy security.

The timing is also political. Fuel prices are at their highest since December 2022, and energy bills are expected to rise this winter amid the Iran conflict. Ministers can point to domestic gas as a response.

The larger test is Rosebank, an oil and gas field described as the UK's last known major untapped oil reserve. No decision has been made. Fahnbulleh has called it a "different proposition" from Jackdaw. Whether the government treats Jackdaw as a one-off or a precedent will show if Trump's compliment was well placed.
trump-burnham-jackdaw.in_one_sentence: Trump praised PM Andy Burnham as 'getting it done' after the government approved the Jackdaw North Sea gas field, a decision that puts Labour's energy stance under fresh scrutiny.

uk-ai-biosecurity-lab.headline: UK to put £100m into 'world first' AI biosecurity lab
uk-ai-biosecurity-lab.body_md:
The UK government says it will put £100m into a laboratory focused on the biological risks that artificial intelligence could create, and it is describing the project as a 'world first'. That is the whole of what has been established so far. The announcement was reported by BBC UK, and this article has not been able to check it against a primary source such as a government statement or a ministerial briefing.

## What is known, and what is not

The figure is £100m, and the stated purpose is biosecurity work with AI at its centre. The 'world first' label is the framing used in the report. It has not been independently confirmed.

The details that would show whether this is a laboratory or a funding label are missing:

- **Location and operator.** Nothing has been confirmed about where the facility would sit or who would run it. A university, a government agency and a defence-science body would each imply a different mission.
- **Timeline.** There is no confirmed opening date, or even a build schedule.
- **Capital versus running costs.** £100m could pay for a building and equipment, or it could fund a research programme for several years. The announcement as reported does not say which.

## The concern behind it

The worry behind projects like this is well documented. Language models and other AI tools can help people with research tasks, and some researchers and officials fear they could also lower the barrier to designing or producing dangerous pathogens. Governments have so far mostly responded by testing AI systems for such abilities and setting rules for the companies that build them. A dedicated public laboratory would be a different kind of response. It would give the state its own place to study the risks hands-on, rather than relying only on what developers choose to disclose.

Whether the UK facility does that is the open question. The phrase 'AI-focused biosecurity lab' could cover several different jobs. One is evaluating AI models for dangerous biological capability. Another is using AI to detect and respond to outbreaks. A third is screening DNA synthesis orders. These are separate activities with separate staff and risks. Until the operator describes the facility's remit, the 'world first' claim cannot be tested. Existing UK and overseas bodies already work on parts of this problem, so the claim would need to rest on something none of them does.

## Why it matters

If the lab is built as described, the significance is less the sum than the signal. £100m is modest next to national science budgets. But a standing facility, as opposed to a time-limited research grant, would suggest that AI-enabled biological risk is being treated as a permanent public-security function. That fits with the broader push to put AI into national-security planning, which Defence Secretary John Healey has said the Budget will advance.

## What to watch

The first test is the official announcement text or ministerial briefing, which should name the host institution, the operator and the split between building and running costs. The second is the Budget itself, where any commitment would have to appear in departmental allocations. Until those arrive, the £100m is a headline number attached to a promising idea.
uk-ai-biosecurity-lab.in_one_sentence: The UK says it will spend £100m on an AI-focused biosecurity lab billed as a 'world first', but location, operator, timeline and the 'world first' claim are all unconfirmed.

texas-sues-openai-altman.headline: Texas sues OpenAI and Altman over alleged harms to users
texas-sues-openai-altman.body_md:
Texas has taken OpenAI to court, and it has named the company's chief executive as a defendant. Attorney General Ken Paxton filed suit on Friday, 23 October, in Collin County district court. It accuses OpenAI and Sam Altman of misleading Texans about ChatGPT and of harming them, children above all. The case tests whether a state can use ordinary consumer-protection law against a generative-AI maker, and whether it can reach the person running the company as well as the company.

## What Texas alleges

The complaint opens with a 2015 remark by Altman: "AI will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there'll be great companies." It goes on to say that OpenAI did not adequately warn users about ChatGPT's risks or about its accuracy. It also says the company knew of the dangers and pressed on in the race to dominate AI.

Paxton's office lists a series of harms. They include mass shooters being aided in deadly rampages, vulnerable people being steered toward suicide, professionals suffering public humiliation, and users losing critical-thinking skills. The office also says minors have become addicted to a tool that "fakes human compassion to collect their data with no parental oversight."

Press reports say the claims rest on the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act. They also cite the state's SCOPE Act, a children's online safety law, with one report saying that claim centres on missing age verification. This article is based on the press release and news coverage. The complaint itself has not been reviewed, so the detail of each claim and the evidence behind the headline harms are not yet known.

## Why Altman is named

The suit seeks to hold Altman personally liable for alleged violations and for statements he made about OpenAI's products. Corporate officers are usually shielded from liability for what their companies do. Consumer-protection suits are a common exception when an executive directs or takes part in the conduct, and Texas appears to be relying on that route. Whether a court will treat Altman's public statements about safety as the kind of conduct that creates personal liability is the most novel question in the case.

The state wants a broad injunction requiring OpenAI to block minors from ChatGPT. It also asks for court-appointed, third-party evaluator approval of any new models. One report puts the monetary relief sought at more than $1 million, a modest figure beside the injunction request. If the court granted the injunction, a judge would in effect be setting conditions for releasing AI models.

## A pattern, and a politician

The suit fits a pattern. In the past year Paxton has sued or settled with Meta, TikTok, Snapchat and Roblox under state consumer-protection laws, arguing their safeguards for children were inadequate. Those cases used familiar legal tools against social platforms. Applying them to a chatbot that generates its own answers is less settled, because it is unclear whether ChatGPT's output is the company's own conduct or something closer to a user's.

The politics are plain. Paxton is running for the US Senate, and the Texas Tribune describes the suit as the latest in a run of actions against large companies. The Tribune also notes that Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI and left in 2018 after a dispute with Altman, is the largest single donor to Paxton's campaign, having given nearly $200 million. Musk later founded the rival xAI. His own 2024 suit against OpenAI and Altman, seeking $1.5 billion, was dismissed by a federal judge. Nothing in the reporting shows Musk had any role in the Texas filing, but the overlap is the kind a defence team will raise. The state's outside counsel includes Ashley Keller and Tony Buzbee, who represented Paxton in his 2023 impeachment proceedings.

## OpenAI's response

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company has worked with experts to reduce risks and add safeguards. The spokesperson added: "Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI." OpenAI said it is willing to work with Texas and other states on policy that applies across the industry. The company has not yet responded to the legal claims in court.

## What to watch

The first signal will be OpenAI's response in Collin County. A motion to dismiss that attacks the claim against Altman personally, or moves the case to federal court, would show where the company thinks the weak points are. Beyond that, other state attorneys general are pursuing OpenAI too. If courts accept that a chatbot's outputs and its makers' safety claims fall under existing deceptive-practices law, states can regulate AI through enforcement without waiting for Congress. If they reject it, the pressure shifts back to legislators.
texas-sues-openai-altman.in_one_sentence: Texas AG Ken Paxton has sued OpenAI and Sam Altman personally, alleging ChatGPT misled users and harmed them, in a test of state consumer-protection law against AI makers.

storm-austen-flood-warning.headline: Storm Austen cuts power to thousands in the south-west as Burnham warns of a 'winter of greater flooding'
storm-austen-flood-warning.body_md:
Storm Austen has left thousands of homes in south-west England without power, and the political reaction has been quicker than the technical detail. Andy Burnham has warned of a "winter of greater flooding" and said he has stockpiled tinned food and bottled water. The remark has put a plain question to ministers and local authorities: are they preparing the public as seriously as some officials say they are preparing themselves?

The evidence behind that question is thin, and the facts below mark where it runs out.

## What is known

The Guardian reports that Storm Austen caused widespread power outages across the south-west, attributing them to strong winds and rain. The reporting available for this article gives no household count beyond "thousands". It also gives no peak gust speeds, no restoration times, and no statement from the network operators. Those figures would show whether this was a routine autumn disruption or something more serious. Storms of this kind regularly bring down lines across the region, and on the information so far Austen fits that pattern.

Burnham's remarks come from reporting by the Guardian and BBC Politics. The headline wording is "winter of greater flooding", and the stockpile is described as including tinned food and bottled water. The exact quote, the setting, and the quantities and timing of the stockpiling have not been independently checked here. They should be read as reported, not as established.

## What is not known

The central gap is the forecast basis. A warning that this winter will bring more flooding than usual carries weight if it rests on Environment Agency or Met Office outlooks. It carries much less if it is a politician's judgment of the mood. The material available contains no flood-risk figures from either body, no seasonal outlook, and no government response. Nor is there any sign of a flood-defence failure linked to Austen.

That shapes how the story should be read. For now it is a political story: a prominent figure has chosen to talk publicly about household resilience. It becomes a preparedness story only if the claim is matched by official forecasts and by evidence about the state of defences, warning systems and grid resilience.

## Why the stockpile matters

The detail of the tinned food gives the warning its force. Official advice in the UK has long encouraged households to keep basic supplies for emergencies. A senior politician saying they have done so turns that advice into a personal example. It also invites the follow-up that critics will press: if the risk is serious enough to act on privately, what is being done publicly, and who is paying for it?

Storm Austen supplies the immediate test of that argument. Power cuts and flooding are linked in practice, because pumping stations, communications and care services all depend on electricity. How quickly supplies are restored, and whether any flooding follows, will say more about resilience than any one politician's pantry.

## What to watch

Three things would settle the matter. First, network operators' final figures on customers affected and the time taken to reconnect them. Second, any Environment Agency or Met Office outlook for the winter, which would show whether the "greater flooding" claim has official backing. Third, a response from ministers on flood-defence funding and emergency planning. Until those arrive, the warning remains a claim to be tested, not a forecast to be relied on.
storm-austen-flood-warning.in_one_sentence: Storm Austen has cut power to thousands in the south-west while Andy Burnham warns of a 'winter of greater flooding', but no official forecast has yet been cited to back the claim.

kompany-hospital-collapse.headline: Bayern boss Kompany taken to hospital after collapsing at training
kompany-hospital-collapse.body_md:
Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital on Friday after collapsing at the club's training ground, a few days before the Bundesliga leaders were due at Freiburg.

The club said the 40-year-old was watching a session involving the reserve team when he collapsed. German broadcaster Sportschau, citing BR24Sport, reported that his condition is stable. Bayern said he is undergoing a thorough examination and will stay under medical care. The club has not given a diagnosis.

## What is known

Kompany had been unwell for about a week with a viral infection. He said he was on the mend after Bayern's Champions League draw with Arsenal on Wednesday, two days before the collapse. Whether the illness and the collapse are connected has not been established, and the club has not said so.

Bayern have taken him out of match operations for now. His coaching staff will run training and matchday duties in the meantime. Sporting director Max Eberl said Kompany would be given as much time as he needs, which suggests the club is not working to a return date.

The reports come from the club's statement as relayed by the BBC, RTÉ, Al Jazeera, ABC and the Washington Post, plus Sportschau. No outlet has yet carried a medical bulletin beyond the word "stable".

## What is not

The gaps matter more than the facts. There is no diagnosis, no timetable for his discharge and no word on who will stand in the dugout at Freiburg on Sunday. Bayern have not said whether an assistant will formally take charge or the staff will share the load.

That last point is the one with sporting consequences. Kompany has run a tightly organised side since arriving in 2024, and a few days of disruption in an otherwise settled season is manageable. A longer absence would be a different matter, and Bayern would then have to name an interim figure and say how long the arrangement lasts.

## What to watch

The first marker is the next club update, which should say whether Kompany has been discharged and whether the viral infection played a part. The second is the team sheet and touchline arrangements for Freiburg on Sunday, which will show who is in charge in his absence. Until then, this is a health scare with a reassuring early word and little else.
kompany-hospital-collapse.in_one_sentence: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany was taken to hospital after collapsing at training; he is reported stable, with no diagnosis and his staff covering matches for now.

ofcom-online-safety-children.headline: Ofcom admits online safety regime has not yet protected children
ofcom-online-safety-children.body_md:
Ofcom, the body charged with policing the UK's Online Safety Act, has said in its own data that the law has not yet made children's online lives measurably safer. Its first report on harmful content, published on 22 October, found "no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content over the first nine months after the children's safety duties came into force in July 2025". The Guardian led its coverage with the admission. The debate has moved from whether platforms are complying to whether the approach works.

## What the report found

Ofcom's survey research put the share of 11- to 17-year-olds who saw harmful content in a four-week period at 73%. The regulator called the finding concerning. It also said it had seen no new evidence that the severity of harm to children had changed.

Two caveats apply. The data cover only the first nine months of the duties. Ofcom said they do not capture the period after it stepped up pressure on Facebook, YouTube, Snap, Roblox and TikTok. And this is survey evidence of what children report seeing, not a count of enforcement actions or removed content, so a flat line does not show that nothing has changed behind the scenes.

The report's one policy recommendation was narrow. Ofcom advised adding body-stigma and depression content to the Act's priority categories of harmful content, and suggested no other changes. It would be for the Secretary of State to adopt that.

## A regulator that was already hedging

The report did not come out of nowhere. In September, Oliver Griffiths, Ofcom's group director for online safety, told the House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee that the regulator was "underwhelmed" by the overall effect so far. Mark Bunting, its director of strategy delivery, said there was "a long way to go".

Ofcom's account of what has worked is specific and limited:

- All of the ten largest pornography services now have age gates.
- Three-quarters of the top 100 services have either introduced age checks or blocked UK users.
- Age checks rose 23-fold across a sample of 32 companies.
- Progress has been slower on the big services children actually use. Ofcom has won commitments from X on removing hate and terrorist content, and from Meta and Snap on grooming risks. It is investigating whether TikTok's age-inference technology missed a "significant proportion" of children. TikTok says it is "confident" it meets its obligations.

Bunting also pointed to a design problem. Platforms can add child protections without having effective ways to identify which users are children. The Act's "safe harbour" can deem a company compliant if it follows Ofcom's codes, even where identified risks remain inadequately addressed. Ofcom suggested the legislation itself may need changing.

## Resources, sequencing and the under-16 ban

The regulator's room to act is also constrained. The Act passed in 2023, and the duties for the largest "categorised services" are not expected to be fully in force until around mid-2027. Ofcom plans to publish a revised roadmap by the end of 2026.

Meanwhile, the government announced in June that it plans to ban under-16s from major social media platforms from next year. Ofcom has moved staff onto implementing that ban, and has asked ministers for more resources in a business plan submitted in July. Griffiths said delivering both the Act and the ban is manageable if properly resourced and sequenced, but warned that without extra staff and funding "something will have to give".

The Children's Commissioner for England, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same inquiry that children felt the Act had made "absolutely no difference". She was reportedly furious that Ofcom had not shared companies' risk assessments with her office. Griffiths said Ofcom had received no formal request and that existing law requires a company's consent before such material goes to a third party. That is a small dispute, but it shows how little outside scrutiny the system allows.

Critics on the free-speech side read the same evidence differently. They argue the Act has age-gated a wide range of content without improving child safety, and that the regulator is seeking to broaden it anyway.

## What to watch

Ofcom has the powers to act. It can fine companies up to £18m or 10% of qualifying worldwide revenue, whichever is higher, and can ultimately seek court orders blocking persistent offenders in Britain. The question now is whether it uses them against the largest services, where the exposure data suggest little has shifted.

Three markers will show which way this goes. The first is the revised roadmap due by the end of the year. The second is the outcome of the TikTok age-inference investigation. The third is the Lords committee's inquiry, which could produce the first formal case for amending the Act, including its safe-harbour provision. Other governments looking to the UK as a model for child-safety rules will be watching how Ofcom answers its own numbers.

spurs-arsenal-derby.headline: Tottenham v Arsenal: north London derby could shape both seasons
spurs-arsenal-derby.body_md:
The north London derby on BBC One this afternoon is the women's one. The men's sides have no league meeting today, and the table says why that matters. The premise that this fixture will "shape both seasons" holds up poorly for the men.

Tottenham Hotspur Women host Arsenal Women in the Women's Super League at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, kick-off 12.45pm BST. Coverage is on BBC One, BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website, according to club and listings sources. Pheobe Cross referees.

## What the tables say

On the men's side, the numbers undercut any talk of a mutual season-definer. As of today, Arsenal are second in the Premier League on 18 points from seven games, three behind unbeaten Manchester City on 21, according to a table published by Swiss outlet nau.ch. Tottenham are 16th on 6 points from seven, with six goals scored and ten conceded. That is a gap of 12 points. It is also a long way from a contest between rivals chasing the same prize.

The women's picture is closer, though not by much. Spurs are fourth in the WSL, five points off the Champions League places, per a preview from the fan site To The Lane And Back. That preview did not give Arsenal's position or points, and a full WSL table was not independently checked for this piece, so how much separates the sides is not established here.

## The women's derby

Spurs started the season well. Manager Martin Ho won the WSL Manager of the Month award for September, but two disappointing results this month have slowed them. Ho has been keen to damp expectations: asked about a top-four finish, he said "we are not at that level". Captain Drew Spence has said the team must fix "a few things" before the derby.

Team news favours neither side. Jess Naz is in contention to return for Spurs after an ACL injury that has kept her out since December 2025, while Olga Ahtinen misses out with a small knock. Arsenal remain without Michelle Agyemang and Katie Reid, both recovering from long-term ACL injuries, and Selia Cerci and Mariona Caldentey are also absent.

## What to watch

For Spurs, the arithmetic is simple. A win would pull them toward the Champions League places they are five points short of, while a second poor result in a few weeks would make Ho's caution look prescient. For Arsenal, the absentees test squad depth early in the season. The men's teams do not meet in the league today. Their next fixtures will show whether Tottenham, 16th and three points above the bottom of the table's relegation-side cluster, are looking up at the derby or down at the drop.
